name: Rene Mott
life: Rene spent a year repairing flood-damaged school papers, most of which nobody famous had touched. He developed a tenderness for cheap glue. It is often the only signature a child leaves on a map. People around the blocks below Foundry Lofts know Rene by a small Monday habit. Rene checks the little hand-lettered notices around Harbour Supply.
voice: My hand shook the day I ruined a school register with too much water. I can lift this page, but the paste itself tells us when it was made. I want photographs before anyone reaches for a brush.
appearance: Rene is easy to recognize by short, uneven waves that refuse to lie flat and a long face and high cheekbones. Usually dressed in a pale blue work shirt with a partly rubbed-away embroidered initial, Rene takes off the watch before a long conversation when listening.
personality: Rene treats keeping somebody waiting as a serious discourtesy. This can turn a helpful person into an impatient one when everybody else needs a slower conversation.
agenda: To document both sides of the handmade page before lifting anything.
family: Charlie Starr is Rene’s cousin. Rene asks before bringing somebody along. Charlie can always ask for five minutes alone. It keeps a conversation between two people from unexpectedly turning into a family committee. Asked about *A room for a father*, Charlie says, “I painted the spare room blue. He called it a color for a nursery and I nearly sent him packing.”
connections: Ona Voss. They compare the age of the paste with the direction of a child's hand stitches.

reactions.situation: A family member disputes the penciled street
reactions.response: Rene marks the disputed piece of street in pencil and keeps the alternative name beside it.

reactions.situation: A traveler asks for the last seat at the bus stop
reactions.response: Rene gives up their own space if possible and asks the passengers who arrived first to choose what happens next.

reactions.response: Rene changes the plan openly and takes responsibility for the delay.
